<fragment>

> Bloom's canon is in many ways mine. It consists of those writers all other writers have to know and by whom they measure themselves. A culture's canon is an evolving consensus of individual canons. Canonical writers changed the medium, the language they were working in. People who merely describe what is happening now don't last. Mine includes writers I don't necessarily like. D. H. Lawrence, though I hate him in a way, Jane Austen, too.[5]
> 
> 

Piotr Wilczek and Adam Czerniawski [pl] criticized Bloom's narrow interpretation of the concept of the West, significantly underrepresenting and even ignoring works from countries he was not familiar with, such as Poland. They interpret his list as dominated by British and American culture, with a small dose of ancient Western classics and a few non-English works from other Western European countries. At the same time, they concur that such a group is pretty standard for the Western canon as understood by most Western European scholars.[6]

<title>The War of the End of the World</title>
<fragment>
[edit]

It is generally believed that Vargas Llosa's three milestone novels are *La Ciudad y Los Perros* (*The Time of the Hero*), *La Casa Verde* (*The Green House*) and *Conversación en la Catedral* (*Conversation in the Cathedral*)[*citation needed*], though many critics agree that *The War of the End of the World* should also be included among these three. The author is famously known for considering this his most accomplished novel[3] — an opinion shared by the Chilean novelist Roberto Bolaño [*citation needed*], as well as the American critic Harold Bloom, who includes the novel in what he calls the "Western canon".


As he did later on with *La Fiesta Del Chivo* (*The Feast of the Goat*), Vargas Llosa tackles a huge number of characters and stories caught during a time of strife, interweaving these in way that gives us a picture of what it was to live in those times.[4]

<title>The War of the End of the World</title>
<fragment>
[edit]

It is generally believed that Vargas Llosa's three milestone novels are *La Ciudad y Los Perros* (*The Time of the Hero*), *La Casa Verde* (*The Green House*) and *Conversación en la Catedral* (*Conversation in the Cathedral*)[*citation needed*], though many critics agree that *The War of the End of the World* should also be included among these three. The author is famously known for considering this his most accomplished novel[3] — an opinion shared by the Chilean novelist Roberto Bolaño [*citation needed*], as well as the American critic Harold Bloom, who includes the novel in what he calls the "Western canon".


As he did later on with *La Fiesta Del Chivo* (*The Feast of the Goat*), Vargas Llosa tackles a huge number of characters and stories caught during a time of strife, interweaving these in way that gives us a picture of what it was to live in those times.[4]

<title>Mario Vargas Llosa</title>
<fragment>
Vargas Llosa has won numerous awards for his writing, from the 1959 *Premio Leopoldo Alas* and the 1962 *Premio Biblioteca Breve* to the 1993 *Premio Planeta* (for *Death in the Andes*) and the Jerusalem Prize in 1995.[173] The literary critic Harold Bloom has included his novel *The War of the End of the World* in his list of essential literary works in the Western Canon.

***The Western Canon: The Books and School of the Ages*** is a 1994 book about Western literature by the American literary critic Harold Bloom, in which the author defends the concept of the Western canon by discussing 26 writers whom he sees as central to the canon.




## Summary

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
Bloom argues against what he calls the "school of resentment", which includes feminist literary criticism, Marxist literary criticism, Lacanians, New Historicism, Deconstructionists, and semioticians. *The Western Canon* includes four appendices listing works that Bloom at the time considered canonical, stretching from the earliest scriptures to Tony Kushner's *Angels in America*. Bloom later disowned the list, saying that it was written at his editor's insistence and distracted from the book's intention.[1]


Bloom defends the concept of the Western canon by discussing 26 writers whom he sees as central to the canon:[2][3]




</fragment>
<fragment>
1. **^** Pearson, James. "Harold Bloom [Interview]". Vice Magazine. Retrieved 23 September 2020.
2. **^** Harold Bloom, *The Western Canon*, 1994, p. 2.
3. **^** Tucker, Ken (21 October 1994). "Book Review: 'The Western Canon: The Books and the School of the Ages'; Books". *EW.com*. Retrieved 1 May 2011.
4. **^** Fruman, Norman (9 October 1994). "Bloom at Thermopylae". *The New York Times*.
5. **^** Lawrence, Tim; Guttridge, Peter. "Reloading the ancient canon". *The Independent* (London). 21 November 1994.
6. ^ ***a*** ***b*** Wilczek, Piotr (2006). "Czy istnieje kanon literatury polskiej?". In Cudak, Romuald (ed.). *Literatura polska w świecie* (in Polish). Wydawnictwo Gnome. pp. 13–23. ISBN 978-83-87819-05-7.
7. **^** Bloom, Harold (1995). *The Western Canon: The Books and School of the Ages*. New York: Riverhead Books. pp. 4, 7, 20, 22, 24, 25, 29, 50, 56, 93, 292, 491, 492. ISBN 978-1-57322-514-4.
8. **^** pdf [*full citation needed*]

</fragment>
<fragment>

> Bloom's canon is in many ways mine. It consists of those writers all other writers have to know and by whom they measure themselves. A culture's canon is an evolving consensus of individual canons. Canonical writers changed the medium, the language they were working in. People who merely describe what is happening now don't last. Mine includes writers I don't necessarily like. D. H. Lawrence, though I hate him in a way, Jane Austen, too.[5]
> 
> 

Piotr Wilczek and Adam Czerniawski [pl] criticized Bloom's narrow interpretation of the concept of the West, significantly underrepresenting and even ignoring works from countries he was not familiar with, such as Poland. They interpret his list as dominated by British and American culture, with a small dose of ancient Western classics and a few non-English works from other Western European countries. At the same time, they concur that such a group is pretty standard for the Western canon as understood by most Western European scholars.[6]


</fragment>

In response, such criticisms have been derided as *ad hominem* and biased in themselves. The counter-argument maintains that such criticisms discount the importance of books solely because of generic, imprecise and possibly irrelevant characteristics of the books' authors, rather than because of the content of the books themselves.[16]



### Works

[edit]

Others thought that while the selected authors were worthy, too much emphasis was placed on the complete works of a single author rather than a wider selection of authors and representative works (for instance, all of Shakespeare's plays are included). <title>The Western Canon</title>
<fragment>
Bloom argues against what he calls the "school of resentment", which includes feminist literary criticism, Marxist literary criticism, Lacanians, New Historicism, Deconstructionists, and semioticians. *The Western Canon* includes four appendices listing works that Bloom at the time considered canonical, stretching from the earliest scriptures to Tony Kushner's *Angels in America*. Bloom later disowned the list, saying that it was written at his editor's insistence and distracted from the book's intention.[1]


Bloom defends the concept of the Western canon by discussing 26 writers whom he sees as central to the canon:[2][3]

***The Western Canon: The Books and School of the Ages*** is a 1994 book about Western literature by the American literary critic Harold Bloom, in which the author defends the concept of the Western canon by discussing 26 writers whom he sees as central to the canon.

> Bloom's canon is in many ways mine. It consists of those writers all other writers have to know and by whom they measure themselves. A culture's canon is an evolving consensus of individual canons. Canonical writers changed the medium, the language they were working in. People who merely describe what is happening now don't last. Mine includes writers I don't necessarily like. D. H. Lawrence, though I hate him in a way, Jane Austen, too.[5]
>

Piotr Wilczek and Adam Czerniawski [pl] criticized Bloom's narrow interpretation of the concept of the West, significantly underrepresenting and even ignoring works from countries he was not familiar with, such as Poland. They interpret his list as dominated by British and American culture, with a small dose of ancient Western classics and a few non-English works from other Western European countries. At the same time, they concur that such a group is pretty standard for the Western canon as understood by most Western European scholars.[6]

![](image)Vargas Llosa in 1982
Vargas Llosa's fourth major novel, *The War of the End of the World* (*La guerra del fin del mundo*), was published in 1981 and was his first attempt at a historical novel.[56] This work initiated a radical change in Vargas Llosa's style towards themes such as messianism and irrational human behaviour.[57] It recreates the War of Canudos, an incident in 19th-century Brazil in which an armed millenarian cult held off a siege by the national army for months.[58] As in Vargas Llosa's earliest work, this novel carries a sober and serious theme, and its tone is dark.[58] Vargas Llosa's bold exploration of humanity's propensity to idealize violence, and his account of a man-made catastrophe brought on by fanaticism on all sides, earned the novel substantial recognition.[59]
Because of the book's ambition and execution, critics have argued that this is one of Vargas Llosa's greatest literary pieces.[59]

Vargas Llosa has won numerous awards for his writing, from the 1959 *Premio Leopoldo Alas* and the 1962 *Premio Biblioteca Breve* to the 1993 *Premio Planeta* (for *Death in the Andes*) and the Jerusalem Prize in 1995.[173] The literary critic Harold Bloom has included his novel *The War of the End of the World* in his list of essential literary works in the Western Canon.


An important distinction he has received is the 1994 Miguel de Cervantes Prize, considered the most important accolade in Spanish-language literature and awarded to authors whose "work has contributed to enrich, in a notable way, the literary patrimony of the Spanish language".[174] In 2002, Vargas was the recipient of the PEN/Nabokov Award. Vargas Llosa also received the 2005 Irving Kristol Award from the American Enterprise Institute and was the 2008 recipient of the Harold and Ethel L. Stellfox Visiting Scholar and Writers Award at Dickinson College.[175]

<document>
<title>Great Books of the Western World</title>
<fragment>

In response, such criticisms have been derided as *ad hominem* and biased in themselves. The counter-argument maintains that such criticisms discount the importance of books solely because of generic, imprecise and possibly irrelevant characteristics of the books' authors, rather than because of the content of the books themselves.[16]



### Works

[edit]

Others thought that while the selected authors were worthy, too much emphasis was placed on the complete works of a single author rather than a wider selection of authors and representative works (for instance, all of Shakespeare's plays are included). The second edition of the set already contained 130 authors and 517 individual works. The editors point out that the guides to additional reading for each topic in the *Syntopicon* refer the interested reader to many more authors.[17]



### Difficulty

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
15. **^** Berlau, John (August 2001). "What Happened to the Great Ideas? – Mortimer J. Adler's Great Books programs". *Insight Magazine Insight on the News*. **17** (32): 16. Archived from the original on 13 March 2014. Retrieved 2 December 2020. Harvard University's Henry Louis Gates blasted the Great Books for showing 'profound disrespect for the intellectual capacities of people of color—red, brown or yellow.'
16. **^** Mortimer Adler (September 1997). "Selecting works for the 1990 edition of Great Books of the Western World". Great Books Index. Archived from the original on 2007-09-27. Retrieved 2007-05-29. We did not base our selections on an author's nationality, religion, politics, or field of study; nor on an author's race or gender. Great books were not chosen to make up quotas of any kind; there was no "affirmative action" in the process.

</fragment>
<fragment>
21. **^** Mortimer J. Adler (1990). "Section 1: The Great Books and the Great Ideas". *The Great Conversation* (2nd ed.). Encyclopædia Britannica, Inc. p. 27. ISBN 0-85229-531-6.

## External links

[edit]

* Center for the Study of the Great Ideas Archived 2021-02-14 at the Wayback Machine Mortimer Adler web pages with extensive discussion of the Great Books
* Greater Books – a site documenting lists of "great books," classics, canons, including the *Great Books of the Western World*
* "Encyclopædia Britannica - Great Books Of The Western World". *Internet Archive*. (54 volumes.)

</fragment>
<fragment>
The second edition of *Great Books of the Western World*, 1990, saw an increase from 54 to 60 volumes, with updated translations. The six new volumes concerned the 20th century, an era of which the first edition's sole representative was Freud. Some of the other volumes were re-arranged, with even more pre-20th century material added but with four texts deleted: Apollonius' *On Conic Sections*, Laurence Sterne's *Tristram Shandy*, Henry Fielding's *Tom Jones*, and Joseph Fourier's *Analytical Theory of Heat*. Adler later expressed regret about dropping *On Conic Sections* and *Tom Jones*. Adler also voiced disagreement with the addition of Voltaire's *Candide*, and said that the Syntopicon should have included references to the Koran. He addressed criticisms that the set was too heavily Western European and did not adequately represent women and minority authors.[11] Four women authors were included, where previously there were none.[12]

<title>Western canon</title>
<fragment>
Some intellectuals have championed a "high conservative modernism" that insists that universal truths exist, and have opposed approaches that deny the existence of universal truths.[8] Yale University Professor of Humanities and famous literary critic Harold Bloom has also argued strongly in favor of the canon, in his 1994 book *The Western Canon: The Books and School of the Ages*, and in general the canon remains as a represented idea in many institutions.[1] Allan Bloom (no relation), in his highly influential *The Closing of the American Mind: How Higher Education Has Failed Democracy and Impoverished the Souls of Today's Students* (1987), argues that moral degradation results from ignorance of the great classics that shaped Western culture. 
</fragment>
<fragment>

For much of the 20th century, the Modern Library provided a larger convenient list of the Western canon, i.e. those books any person (or any English-speaking person) needed to know in order to claim an excellent general education. The list numbered more than 300 items by the 1950s, by authors from Aristotle to Albert Camus, and has continued to grow. When in the 1990s the concept of the Western canon was vehemently condemned, just as earlier Modern Library lists had been criticized as "too American," Modern Library responded by preparing new lists of "100 Best Novels" and "100 Best Nonfiction" compiled by famous writers, and later compiled lists nominated by book purchasers and readers.[7]



### Debate

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

The terms "classic book" and Western canon are closely related concepts, but are not necessarily synonymous. A "canon" is a list of books considered to be "essential", and it can be published as a collection (such as *Great Books of the Western World*, Modern Library, Everyman's Library or Penguin Classics), presented as a list with an academic's imprimatur (such as Harold Bloom's[4]), or be the official reading list of a university. In *The Western Canon* Bloom lists "the major Western writers" as Dante Alighieri, Geoffrey Chaucer, Miguel de Cervantes, Michel de Montaigne, William Shakespeare, Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, William Wordsworth, Charles Dickens, Leo Tolstoy, James Joyce and Marcel Proust.

## Key Findings:

### **"The War of the End of the World" in Bloom's Canon** ✅

Harold Bloom definitively includes Mario Vargas Llosa's novel "The War of the End of the World" in his Western canon. This is **explicitly confirmed** in multiple sources:

From the Wikipedia article on *Mario Vargas Llosa*:
> "The literary critic Harold Bloom has included his novel *The War of the End of the World* in his list of essential literary works in the Western Canon."

From the Wikipedia article on *The War of the End of the World*:
> "...the American critic Harold Bloom, who includes the novel in what he calls the 'Western canon'"

### **About Bloom's "The Western Canon" (1994)**

He writes, prolifically, across an array of literary genres, including literary criticism and journalism. His novels include comedies, murder mysteries, historical novels, and political thrillers. Several, such as *Captain Pantoja and the Special Service* (1973/1978) and *Aunt Julia and the Scriptwriter* (1977/1982), have been adapted as feature films.


</fragment>
<fragment>

Most of Vargas Llosa's narratives have been translated into multiple languages, marking his international critical success.[165] Vargas Llosa is also noted for his substantial contribution to journalism, an accomplishment characteristic of few other Latin American writers.[168] He is recognized among those who have most consciously promoted literature in general, and more specifically the novel itself, as avenues for meaningful commentary about life.[169] During his career, he has written more than a dozen novels and many other books and stories, and, for decades, he has been a voice for Latin American literature.[170]


</fragment>
<fragment>

A number of Vargas Llosa's works have been adapted for the screen, including *The Time of the Hero* and *Captain Pantoja and the Special Service* (both by the Peruvian director Francisco Lombardi) and *The Feast of the Goat* (by Vargas Llosa's cousin, Luis Llosa).[171] *Aunt Julia and the Scriptwriter* was turned into the English-language film, *Tune in Tomorrow*. *The Feast of the Goat* has also been adapted as a theatrical play by Jorge Alí Triana, a Colombian playwright and director.[172]



## Awards and honors

[edit]

From upper left: *Honoris Causa* Doctorate from Harvard University; *Honoris Causa* Doctorate from University of Cambridge; *Honoris Causa* Doctorate and Bachelor's degree from National University of San Marcos, his *alma mater*; Nobel Prize in Literature Medal and Diploma.


</fragment>
<fragment>
Vargas Llosa has won numerous awards for his writing, from the 1959 *Premio Leopoldo Alas* and the 1962 *Premio Biblioteca Breve* to the 1993 *Premio Planeta* (for *Death in the Andes*) and the Jerusalem Prize in 1995.[173] The literary critic Harold Bloom has included his novel *The War of the End of the World* in his list of essential literary works in the Western Canon.


An important distinction he has received is the 1994 Miguel de Cervantes Prize, considered the most important accolade in Spanish-language literature and awarded to authors whose "work has contributed to enrich, in a notable way, the literary patrimony of the Spanish language".[174] In 2002, Vargas was the recipient of the PEN/Nabokov Award. Vargas Llosa also received the 2005 Irving Kristol Award from the American Enterprise Institute and was the 2008 recipient of the Harold and Ethel L. Stellfox Visiting Scholar and Writers Award at Dickinson College.[175]

[edit]

It is generally believed that Vargas Llosa's three milestone novels are *La Ciudad y Los Perros* (*The Time of the Hero*), *La Casa Verde* (*The Green House*) and *Conversación en la Catedral* (*Conversation in the Cathedral*)[*citation needed*], though many critics agree that *The War of the End of the World* should also be included among these three. <document>
<title>Latin American Boom</title>
<fragment>
![Greying man deep in concentration.](image)Mario Vargas Llosa
Mario Vargas Llosa is a Peruvian novelist, short story writer, playwright, journalist and literary and political critic.[41] He attended Lima's University of San Marcos and subsequently attained a doctorate in Latin American literature in Spain.[42] In fact, his thesis was on Gabriel García Márquez.[43] He shot to fame with his novel *The Time of the Hero* (1963), a scathing indictment of cruelty and corruption in a Peruvian military academy (and, by implication, in Peruvian society).


Vargas Llosa also wrote *The Green House* (1966), the epic Conversation in the Cathedral (1969), Captain Pantoja and the Special Service (1973), and post-Boom novels such as Aunt Julia and the Scriptwriter (1977). Vargas Llosa returned to Lima in 2000, following the resignation of President Fujimori who won the 1990 Peruvian election, beating Vargas Llosa.[43] The Swedish Academy awarded him the 2010 Nobel Prize in Literature.




## Other figures

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

He is best known for novels such as *One Hundred Years of Solitude* (1967) and *The Autumn of the Patriarch* (1975), *No One Writes to the Colonel* (1962), and post-Boom work such as *Love in the Time of Cholera* (1985). He has achieved significant critical acclaim and widespread commercial success, most notably for introducing what has been labeled magical realism to the literary world. He experimented with more or less traditional approaches to reality, so that "the most frightful, the most unusual things are told with the deadpan expression".[40] A commonly cited example is the physical and spiritual ascending into heaven of a character while she is hanging the laundry out to dry in *One Hundred Years of Solitude.* García Márquez is now considered one of the most significant authors of the 20th century, as is attested by his winning the 1982 Nobel Prize in Literature. García Márquez died on April 17, 2014.




### Mario Vargas Llosa

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

This period saw the publishing of Boom novels in Barcelona, reflecting the new interest of Spanish publishing houses in the Spanish American market. However, as Alejandro Herrero-Olaizola notes, the revenue generated by the publishing of these novels gave a boost to the Spanish economy, even as the works were subjected to Franco's censors.[46] Some of the Seix Barral-published novels include Mario Vargas Llosa's *The Time of the Hero* (1963) and his *Captain Pantoja and the Special Service* (1973), and Manuel Puig's *Betrayed by Rita Hayworth* (1971).[47] A crucial figure "in the promotion of Latin American literature in Spain" (and elsewhere) was the "super-agent" Carmen Balcells, whom Vargas Llosa referred to as "The Big Mama of the Latin American novel."[48]



## Critique

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Fuentes not only wrote some of the most important novels of the period, but was also a critic and publicist of Spanish America. In 1955 Fuentes and Emmanuel Carballo founded the journal *Revista Mexicana de Literatura* which introduced Latin Americans to the works of European Modernists and the ideas of Jean-Paul Sartre and Albert Camus.[36] In 1969 he published the important critical work, *La nueva novela hispanoamericana*. Fuentes held the position of professor of Latin American literature at Columbia University (1978) and at Harvard (1987)[37] and more recently was associated with Brown University. He once said that "the so-called Boom, in reality, is the result of four centuries that, literarily, reached a moment of urgency in which fiction became the way to organize lessons from the past."[38] Fuentes died on May 15, 2012.

***The Time of the Hero*** (Original title: *La ciudad y los perros*, literally "The City and the Dogs") is a 1963 novel by Peruvian writer and Nobel laureate Mario Vargas Llosa. It was Vargas Llosa's first novel and is set among the cadets at the Leoncio Prado Military Academy in Lima, which he attended as a teenager. The novel portrays the school so scathingly that its leadership burned many copies and condemned the book as Ecuadorian propaganda against Peru.[1]


It won the 1962 Premio Biblioteca Breve for best unpublished novel[2] and the 1963 Premio de la Crítica Española.[3]




## Style and themes

[edit]

The novel is notable for its experimental and complex employment of multiple perspectives in a non-linear fashion.[3] A technique influenced by William Faulkner and particularly the novel *Light in August*.[4]


</fragment>
<fragment>

It is a story about adolescence and young males transition to manhood, but is also described to portray a microcosm of the Peruvian society. It features themes such as masculinity, hierarchy, secrecy and the military.[3]



## Plot summary

[edit]

The story concerns the theft of an examination paper by the cadet Cava carried out under orders from Jaguar, the brutal leader of a group of cadets called The Circle. The theft is reported by a lowly cadet called The Slave whom Jaguar consequently murders during military maneuvers. Concerned for the school’s reputation, the administrators choose to ignore further evidence of Jaguar’s guilt.



## Background

[edit]

The novel is based on Vargas Llosa's own experiences of Leoncio Prado Military Academy, which he attended as a teenager in the early 1950s. He worked on the manuscript for the novel while he was living in France and it was published as his first novel in 1962.[3]

The protagonist of the novel, Santiago Zavala, is a student of the National University of San Marcos in Lima and an activist with the group Cahuide against the dictatorship of the government of Peru; Santiago is based on some real life experiences of Vargas Llosa, during his first years at University of San Marcos and as a member of the activist group Cahuide. More generally, the novel is an examination of the deep roots of corruption and failure in Peruvian politics and government during the 1950s. ***Conversation in The Cathedral*** (original title: *Conversación en La catedral*) is a 1969 novel by Spanish-Peruvian writer and essayist Mario Vargas Llosa, translated by Gregory Rabassa. One of Vargas Llosa's major works, it is a portrayal of Peru under the dictatorship of Manuel A. Odría in the 1950s, and deals with the lives of characters from different social strata.[1] The ambitious narrative is built around the stories of Santiago Zavala and Ambrosio respectively; one the son of a minister, the other the minister's chauffeur.[2] A random meeting at a dog pound leads to a riveting conversation between the two at a nearby bar known as The Cathedral (hence the title).[3] During the encounter Zavala tries to find the truth about his father's role in the murder of a notorious Peruvian underworld figure, shedding light on the workings of a dictatorship along the way.

***Aunt Julia and the Scriptwriter*** (Template:Lang-es) is the seventh novel by Nobel Prize-winning author Mario Vargas Llosa. It was published by Seix Barral, S.A., Spain, in 1977. 




## Plot

[edit]

Set in Peru during the 1950s, it is the story of an 18-year-old student who falls for a 32-year-old divorcee. The novel is based on the author's real life experience.


Mario, an aspiring writer, works at a radio station, Panamericana, writing news bulletins alongside the disaster-obsessed Pascual. Mario has an aunt (married to a biological uncle) whose sister, Julia, has just been divorced and has come to live with some of his family members. He frequently sees her and though at first they do not get on, they start to go to movies together and gradually become romantically involved, ultimately getting married. 


Mario's bosses also run Panamericana's sister station, which broadcasts *novelas* (short-run soap operas). They are having problems buying the serials in bulk from Cuba, with batches of scripts being ruined and quality being poor, and so they hire an eccentric Bolivian scriptwriter named Pedro Camacho to write the serials.


The novel chronicles the scriptwriter's rise in popularity, and subsequent descent into madness, in tandem with the protagonist's affair. It alternates between Mario's account of his life and episodes of Camacho's serials, which become increasingly unhinged as the novel progresses.



## Background

[edit]

The novel is based in part on the author's first marriage, to Julia Urquidi. Urquidi later wrote a memoir, *Lo que Varguitas no dijo* (*What little Vargas didn't say*), in which she provided her own version of their relationship.


Vargas Llosa's novel was later adapted as a Hollywood feature film, *Tune in Tomorrow*, in which the setting was moved from Lima to New Orleans. The film was released as *Aunt Julia and the Scriptwriter* in many countries.[1]

<document>
<title>2010 Nobel Prize in Literature</title>
<fragment>
Mario Vargas Llosa was one of the leading writers in the Latin American boom. His extensive, rich authorship consists mostly of novels, but also of plays, essays, literary criticisms, and journalism. His major breakthroughs include *La ciudad y los perros* (lit. "The City and the Dogs"/trans. "The Time of the Hero", 1963), *La casa verde* ("The Green House", 1965), *La guerra del fin del mundo* ("The War of the End of the World", 1984), and the monumental *Conversación en la catedral* ("Conversation in the Cathedral", 1969). His works reflect his ardent love of storytelling. They are characterized by rich language and cover a range of genres—from autobiographical books and historical novels to erotic fiction and thrillers such as *La tía Julia y el escribidor* ("Aunt Julia and the Scriptwriter", 1982) and *Travesuras de la niña mala* ("The Bad Girl", 2007). 
</fragment>
<fragment>

> "Mario Vargas Llosa's writing has shaped our image of South America and has its own chapter in the history of contemporary literature. In his early years, he was a renewer of the novel; today, an epic poet of not only Latin American stature. His wide embrace enfolds all literary genres.", "Vargas Llosa has led us through unfamiliar milieux with an authority that lends the authenticity of a 19th-century explorer. He links the narrative tradition of Balzac and Tolstoy to the modernistic experiments of William Faulkner." 
> 
>

Vargas Llosa's first novel, *The Time of the Hero* (*La ciudad y los perros*), was published in 1963. ## Publication Details

*The Time of the Hero* (Original title: *La ciudad y los perros*, literally "The City and the Dogs") is Mario Vargas Llosa's first novel, published in 1963. The novel won two prestigious awards:
- The 1962 Premio Biblioteca Breve for best unpublished novel
- The 1963 Premio de la Crítica Española

Vargas Llosa worked on the manuscript while living in France, and it was published to immediate success and wide public attention.

## Plot Summary

The novel is set among cadets at the Leoncio Prado Military Academy in Lima, Peru. The central story involves:

1. **The Theft**: Cadet Cava steals an examination paper under orders from Jaguar, the brutal leader of a group called "The Circle"

2. **The Murder**: The theft is reported by a low-ranking cadet called "The Slave," whom Jaguar consequently murders during military maneuvers

3. **The Cover-up**: School administrators, concerned about the institution's reputation, choose to ignore further evidence of Jaguar's guilt and cover up the crime

## Background

The novel is semi-autobiographical, based on Vargas Llosa's own experiences attending Leoncio Prado Military Academy as a teenager in the early 1950s. This personal connection lends authenticity to the brutal portrayal of military school life.

## Key Themes

The novel explores several major themes:

- **Adolescence and masculinity**: The story addresses young males' transition to manhood in a harsh military environment
- **Hierarchy and power**: It examines the brutal hierarchies and power structures within the military academy
- **Secrecy and corruption**: The military institution is portrayed as corrupt, with administrators covering up crimes
- **Social microcosm**: The school serves as a microcosm of Peruvian society, reflecting broader social corruption

## Literary Significance and Style

*The Time of the Hero* is considered a landmark work for several reasons:

1. **Experimental Narrative**: The novel is notable for its complex, non-linear narrative structure using multiple perspectives
2. **Literary Influences**: The technique was influenced by William Faulkner, particularly his novel *Light in August*
3. **Latin American Boom**: It helped establish Vargas Llosa as a major figure in the Latin American Boom literary movement
4. **Critical Acclaim**: The novel impressed critics with its vitality and sophisticated literary techniques

## Reception and Controversy

The novel received both acclaim and intense controversy:

**Positive Reception:**
- Won two major literary awards
- Gained immediate international success
- Praised for its sophisticated style and social critique

**Controversy:**
- Peruvian military establishment harshly criticized the novel
- Several Peruvian generals attacked it as the work of a "degenerate mind"
- Vargas Llosa was accused of being "paid by Ecuador" to undermine the Peruvian Army
- The military academy leadership burned many copies and condemned the book as propaganda against Peru

## Notable Adaptations

The novel was adapted into a film in 1985 by Peruvian director Francisco Lombardi, titled *La ciudad y los perros*.

## Historical Context

The novel was published during a significant period in Latin American literature - the early 1960s - when writers like Vargas Llosa were challenging traditional narrative forms and addressing pressing social and political issues through fiction. This work, along with his subsequent novels *The Green House* (1966) and *Conversation in the Cathedral* (1969), established Vargas Llosa as one of the leading figures of the Latin American Boom and contributed to his eventual reception of the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2010.

The novel remains one of Vargas Llosa's most important early works, celebrated for both its literary innovation and its powerful social critique of Peruvian society and its institutions.

***The Green House*** (Original title: *La Casa Verde*) is the second novel by the Peruvian writer Mario Vargas Llosa, published in 1966. The novel is set over a period of forty years (from the early part of the 20th century to the 1960s) in two regions of Peru: Piura, a dusty town near the coast in the north, and Peruvian Amazonia, specifically the jungle region near the Marañón river.




## Background

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Vargas Llosa adds to this narrative complexity by referring to characters obliquely ("the lieutenant", "the native", etc.) and by telling the story non-chronologically (parallel narratives may be decades apart). He also creates double narratives within chapters without clear demarcation. The effect is to interweave past and present and to suggest an omnipresent and continuing corruption and brutality.



## Plot synopsis

[edit]

**In the desert:**


During the early years of the 20th century, a mysterious stranger named Anselmo, whose origins and motives are never explained, builds a popular brothel, the Green House, in the desert on the outskirts of Piura.


</fragment>
<fragment>
The novel was inspired by memories of the author's youth in Piura and a journey through the jungle he made in 1958. Vargas Llosa has described the novel as "a fusion of very different experiences" that had impressed him.[1]


</fragment>
<fragment>
* Sergeant Lituma: a resident of Piura and husband of Bonifacia, he serves in the Peruvian military in the Amazonia region before returning to his home town.
* Adrian Nieves: a river pilot involved in the capture of Bonifacia, he works for Fushia and has three children with Lalita.
* Julio Reategui: the son of a rubber merchant, he colludes with Fushia on the illegal rubber trade and becomes provincial Governor.

The protagonist of the novel, Santiago Zavala, is a student of the National University of San Marcos in Lima and an activist with the group Cahuide against the dictatorship of the government of Peru; Santiago is based on some real life experiences of Vargas Llosa, during his first years at University of San Marcos and as a member of the activist group Cahuide. In the novel, the protagonist Santiago Zavala depicts a pessimistic view of Peruvian society during the 1950s, at the same time he is embracing the mediocrity. More generally, the novel is an examination of the deep roots of corruption and failure in Peruvian politics and government during the 1950s. The second sentence of the English translation of the novel poses the question "At what precise moment had Peru fucked itself up?"[4]

***Conversation in The Cathedral*** (original title: *Conversación en La catedral*) is a 1969 novel by Spanish-Peruvian writer and essayist Mario Vargas Llosa, translated by Gregory Rabassa. One of Vargas Llosa's major works, it is a portrayal of Peru under the dictatorship of Manuel A. Odría in the 1950s, and deals with the lives of characters from different social strata.[1] The ambitious narrative is built around the stories of Santiago Zavala and Ambrosio respectively; one the son of a minister, the other the minister's chauffeur.[2] A random meeting at a dog pound leads to a riveting conversation between the two at a nearby bar known as The Cathedral (hence the title).[3] During the encounter Zavala tries to find the truth about his father's role in the murder of a notorious Peruvian underworld figure, shedding light on the workings of a dictatorship along the way.

基于我的研究，我为您提供关于马里奥·巴尔加斯·略萨2010年诺贝尔文学奖及其主要作品的全面信息：

## **2010年诺贝尔文学奖成就**

马里奥·巴尔加斯·略萨于2010年获得诺贝尔文学奖，瑞典学院授予他这一荣誉的重要理由包括：

**官方评语**：
- "for his cartography of structures of power and his trenchant images of the individual's resistance, revolt, and defeat"
（"因其对权力结构的地图绘制及其对个人反抗、起义和失败的犀利刻画"）

**瑞典学院的具体评价**：
- "Mario Vargas Llosa's writing has shaped our image of South America and has its own chapter in the history of contemporary literature"
- "In his early years, he was a renewer of the novel; today, an epic poet of not only Latin American stature"
- "He links the narrative tradition of Balzac and Tolstoy to the modernistic experiments of William Faulkner"
- "Vargas Llosa has led us through unfamiliar milieux with an authority that lends the authenticity of a 19th-century explorer"

---

## **基础完成作品（四大里程碑小说）**

### **1. 《城市与狗》（The Time of the Hero, 1963）**

**背景与意义**：
- 略萨的首部小说，为其奠定文学声誉
- 获1962年 literary奖项
- 被视为拉美文学爆炸的重要作品

**故事背景**：
- 设定在利马的 Leoncio Prado 军事学院（基于略萨个人经历）
- 揭示军事教育中的暴力和腐败

**主要冲突**：
- 学员 Cava 被迫偷考卷事件
- 弱小学员"奴隶"被残忍杀害
- 学校管理者为声誉掩盖真相

**文学技巧**：
- 采用多角度叙事和非线性时间结构
- 受福克纳影响，采用意识流手法
- 奠定其"多声道"叙事风格

**争议影响**：
- 在秘鲁引起军方强烈反弹
- 被指责诋毁秘鲁军队形象
- 多部小说被军方焚烧

---

### **2. 《绿房子》（The Green House, 1966）**

**叙事结构**：
- 时间跨度40年（20世纪初至1960年代）
- 双线叙事：皮乌拉沙漠地区 vs 亚马逊雨林
- 更加复杂的时空交错技巧

**核心内容**：
- 神秘人 Anselmo 在沙漠边缘建立妓院"绿房子"
- 亚马逊地区的橡胶贸易和冲突
- 展现秘鲁不同地区的社会全貌

**文学成就**：
- 进一步发展其复调小说技巧
- 被认为是他最具实验性的作品之一
- 体现其将个人经历与历史现实融合的能力

---

### **3. 《教堂中的对话》（Conversation in the Cathedral, 1969）**

**主题背景**：
- 描绘秘鲁在独裁者 Manuel Odría 统治下的1950年代
- 著名的开篇句："At what precise moment had Peru fucked itself up?"（秘鲁究竟在哪个准确的时刻搞砸了？）

**叙事结构**：
- 两个主角：政府部长之子 Santiago Zavala 和部长司机 Ambrosio
- 随机相遇引发的长篇对话，揭露政治腐败真相
- 多层次、多角度的社会全景式描写

**政治深度**：
- 深刻揭示独裁政治的运作机制
- 展现权力如何渗透社会各个层面
- 被认为是他最具政治深度的作品

---

### **4. 《世界末日之战》（The War of the End of the World, 1981）**

**历史背景**：
- 基于19世纪末巴西真实的"卡努杜斯战争"
- 农民宗教运动与政府的残酷镇压

**作者观点**：
- 略萨本人认为这是他"最完美的作品"
- 智利作家波拉尼奥和评论家布鲁姆也给予极高评价
- 许多批评家认为应与前三部并列为"四部杰作"

**艺术成就**：
- 史诗般的叙事规模
- 宏大历史事件与个人命运的完美结合
- 获得 PEN 翻译奖等重要文学奖项

---

## **诺贝尔文学奖获奖的深层原因**

### **1. 文学创新**
- 重新定义了拉丁美洲小说的形式
- 融合现实主义与现代主义技巧
- 发展出独特的"多声道"叙事结构

### **2. 社会批判**
- 深刻描绘拉美社会的权力结构
- 为被压迫者和边缘群体发声
- 揭示政治腐败和社会不公

### **3. 全球影响**
- 作品被翻译成多种语言
- 影响世界文学发展
- 成为世界文学经典

### **4. 人文关怀**
- "Vargas Llosa believes in the force of literature"（略萨相信文学的力量）
- 认为文学是反对偏见、种族主义和狭隘民族主义的堡垒
- 坚持为言论自由和人权而斗争

---

## **作品的时间脉络与文学意义**

**1963-1969**：早期实验期，建立叙事创新
**1970年代**：题材拓展，政治参与加深
**1981**：史诗般的《世界末日之战》，达到艺术巅峰
**1980年代后期**：转向更个人化的主题
**2000年后**：历史小说与现实关注并重

这四部早期作品构成了略萨文学成就的核心foundation，它们不仅确立了他作为拉丁美洲文学大师的地位，也为他获得诺贝尔文学奖奠定了坚实的文学基础。这些作品展现了他将个人经历、历史现实和文学技巧完美融合的独特能力，使其成为当代世界文学最重要的人物之一。

<title>Tomas Tranströmer</title>
<fragment>
Tranströmer is considered to be one of the "most influential Scandinavian poet[s] of recent decades".[5] Tranströmer published 15 collected works over his extensive career, which have been translated into over 60 languages.[5] An English translation by Robin Fulton of his entire body of work, *New Collected Poems*, was published in the UK in 1987 and expanded in 1997. Following the publication of *The Great Enigma*, Fulton's edition was further expanded into *The Great Enigma: New Collected Poems,* published in the US in 2006 and as an updated edition of *New Collected Poems*[9] in the UK in 2011. He published a short autobiography, *Minnena ser mig* *(The Memories see me)*, in 1993.

***17 Poems*** (Template:Lang-sv) is a 1954 poetry collection by the Swedish writer Tomas Tranströmer. It was Tranströmer's debut book: he had previously only been published in journals.[1] The book was well received in the Swedish press and praised for its formal confidence and imagination in metaphors.[2]


Several of the poems in 17 poems have been set to music.[3][4]

***The Sorrow Gondola*** (Template:Lang-sv) is a 1996 poetry collection by the Swedish writer Tomas Tranströmer. The title refers to the composition *La lugubre gondola* by Franz Liszt. It was the first collection by Tranströmer published after his 1990 stroke. It received the August Prize.[1]



## Reception

[edit]

The book was reviewed in *Publishers Weekly*, where the critic wrote that while the author's stroke is never mentioned explicitly, the collection "centers unmistakably on the controlled anguish that the 66-year-old poet's physical condition--and encroaching mortality--imposes." The review continued: "What saves the collection from morbidness is the formal beauty and remorselessly compressed clarity of the writing. Indeed, the almost telegraphic brevity of the poems is the volume's only concession to Transtromer's handicap. With the exception of the four-page title poem, a meditation on Wagner's final months, most of the pieces are only a few stanzas long, yet they retain all the force of the poet's earlier work."[2]

<title>2011 Nobel Prize in Literature</title>
<fragment>
Tomas Tranströmer has this ability to draw out the great and wonderful from the mundane. Since his writing debut in the 1950s with *17 dikter* ("17 Poems", 1954) and *Hemligheter på vägen* ("Secrets on the Way", 1958), Tranströmer's poetry has been characterized by its "everyday roots", and a striving after simplicity that allows room for its reader to marvel and to concentrate.[2] His poems are marked by rich, keen and original imagery. Two of Tranströmer's greatest interests, nature and music, have also left deep impressions on his writing. His famous literary collections include *Östersjöar* ("Baltics", 1974), *För levande och döda* ("For the Living and the Dead", 1989), *Sorgegondolen* ("The Sorrow Gondola", 1996), and *Den stora gåtan* ("The Great Enigma", 2004).[4][3]

***The Sorrow Gondola*** (Template:Lang-sv) is a 1996 poetry collection by the Swedish writer Tomas Tranströmer. The title refers to the composition *La lugubre gondola* by Franz Liszt. It was the first collection by Tranströmer published after his 1990 stroke. It received the August Prize.[1]



## Reception

[edit]

The book was reviewed in *Publishers Weekly*, where the critic wrote that while the author's stroke is never mentioned explicitly, the collection "centers unmistakably on the controlled anguish that the 66-year-old poet's physical condition--and encroaching mortality--imposes." The review continued: "What saves the collection from morbidness is the formal beauty and remorselessly compressed clarity of the writing. Indeed, the almost telegraphic brevity of the poems is the volume's only concession to Transtromer's handicap. With the exception of the four-page title poem, a meditation on Wagner's final months, most of the pieces are only a few stanzas long, yet they retain all the force of the poet's earlier work."[2]

*Svenska Dagbladet'*s critic wrote: "When reading [the first five poems] you are delighted by the natural easiness which always has characterised Tranströmer's poetry, in the following haikus by the formal restraint and discipline which makes up the other side of his authorship - not a word too much!" The critic continued: "Tranströmer's new poems are permeated by a completely natural piety. No high tones, no preachment! Only a calm confidence before mortality and a through and through unsentimentally formulated gratitude for being able to exist, to participate."[1]


The book was nominated for the August Prize.[6] In 2007, Frie, whose painting is on the book's cover, collaborated with Tranströmer and exhibited 13 original landscape paintings inspired by the book.[4]

In November 1990, Tomas Tranströmer suffered a stroke which paralysed the right side of his body and damaged his ability to speak. He therefore had to cancel a large-scale poetry project he was working on, about the history of Europe, to instead write more concise poems. Several times he considered to quit writing altogether, but kept coming up with new ideas. He returned to the haiku format, which he according to himself had been both reading and writing for his whole life. His earliest published haiku were written in 1959, when he worked at a youth prison, and in 1996 he published the collection *The Sorrow Gondola* which contained eleven more. ## Complete Bibliography of Tomas Tranströmer's Original Poetry Collections (in Swedish)

Based on the search results and known information about Tranströmer's work, here are his major poetry collections in Swedish with their original publication dates:

### 1950s-1960s
1. **17 dikter** (17 Poems) - 1954
   - His debut collection, published when he was 23
   - Received widespread critical acclaim for its formal confidence and metaphorical imagination

2. **Hemligheter på vägen** (Secrets on the Way) - 1958

### 1970s

7. **Östersjöar** (Baltics) - 1974
8. **Sanningar på gatan** (Truths in the Street) - 1978

### 1980s-1990s
9. **Det vilda torget** (The Wild Square) - 1983
10. **För levande och döda** (For the Living and the Dead) - 1989
    - This collection won the Nordic Council Literature Prize

11. **Sorgegondolen** (The Sorrow Gondola) - 1996
    - His first collection after his 1990 stroke
    - Won the August Prize (Sweden's most prestigious literary award)
    - Written slowly with his left hand due to paralysis

### 2000s
12. **Den stora gåtan** (The Great Enigma) - 2004
    - His second collection after the stroke
    - Consists of 5 free-format poems followed by 45 haiku in 11 suites
    - Written with left hand at a slow pace
    - Nominated for the August Prize

## Critical Reception and Literary Assessment

### Awards and Recognition
- **Nobel Prize in Literature (2011)** - The highest international recognition
- **August Prize (1996)** - For *The Sorrow Gondola*
- **Nordic Council Literature Prize (1990)** - For *För levande och döda*
- **Numerous international poetry prizes**

### Critical Themes and Assessment
From the search results, I can identify several key aspects of his critical reception:

1. **Post-Stroke Mastery**: Critics particularly praised *The Sorrow Gondola* (1996) for how it dealt with "controlled anguish" and "encroaching mortality" while maintaining "formal beauty and remorselessly compressed clarity." The review in Publishers Weekly noted that the poems' "almost telegraphic brevity" was the only concession to his physical handicap.

2. **Natural Piety**: *The Great Enigma* (2004) was described by *Svenska Dagbladet* as being "permeated by a completely natural piety" with "no high tones, no preachment!" but rather "a calm confidence before mortality and a through and through unsentimentally formulated gratitude for being able to exist."

3. **Formal Innovation**: Critics consistently noted his mastery of both free verse and haiku forms, with the haiku following traditional 5-7-5 syllable structure while maintaining his characteristic clarity and precision.

### Key Poetic Characteristics (Based on Critical Assessment)
- **Metaphorical imagination and formal confidence** (from debut collection reviews)
- **Compressed clarity and formal beauty** 
- **Natural, unsentimental approach to mortality**
- **Integration of music and landscape imagery**
- **Psychological depth** (reflecting his background as a psychologist)

### Scholarly Significance
Tranströmer is considered one of the most important Swedish poets of the 20th century, bridging modernist and contemporary poetry. His work has been translated into over 60 languages, and he's frequently cited when the Swedish Academy considers candidates for the Nobel Prize in Literature.

## Notable Translated Collections
The search results also show extensive translation activity, with major English collections including:
- *The Great Enigma: New Collected Poems* (2006)
- *The Sorrow Gondola* (1997)
- *For the Living and the Dead* (1994)
- *The Half-Finished Heaven* (2001)

This bibliography demonstrates Tranströmer's enduring influence on world poetry and the remarkable critical acclaim he received throughout his career, particularly for his ability to maintain poetic mastery even after his debilitating stroke.

<title>Swedish literature</title>
<fragment>
Arguably the most famous Swedish poet of the 20th century is Tomas Tranströmer (1931–2015). His poetry is distinguished by a Christian mysticism, moving on the verge between dream and reality, the physical and the metaphysical.[54] At the same time there in the Sixties developed a strong tradition influenced by the historical avant-garde, and the Swedish movement of concrete poetry became one of the three global representants for experimental poetry at this time, with representatives like Öyvind Fahlström (who seemingly published the first manifesto for concrete poetry in the world 1954: "Hätila ragulpr på fåtskliaben"),[55] Åke Hodell, Bengt Emil Johnson, and Leif Nylén. In a reaction against the experimental Sixties one in the Seventies took up the beat-tradition from the US, in a continued avant-garde effort which resulted in little magazines publishing poetry, a stencil movement out of which one of Swedish main poets of today – Bruno K. 
</fragment>
<fragment>

The literature of the 1950s continued some of the themes of the 1940s but became more ironic and playful with writers such as Lars Gyllensten, Willy Kyrklund and Lars Forssell. Birgitta Trotzig, a major modernist writer whose work focus on existential questions of a religions nature made her breakthrough with *De utsatta* (*The Exposed*) in 1957. Poets associated with the 1950s are Werner Aspenström who became one of the most widely read poets in Sweden and the highly influential Tomas Tranströmer who made his debut in 1954 with *17 dikter* (*17 Poems*).[45]

Tranströmer was born in Stockholm in 1931 and raised by his mother Helmy, a schoolteacher, following her divorce from his father, Gösta Tranströmer, an editor.[5][6] He received his secondary education at the Södra Latin Gymnasium in Stockholm, where he began writing poetry. In addition to selected journal publications, his first collection of poems, *17 Poems*, was published in 1954. ***17 Poems*** (Template:Lang-sv) is a 1954 poetry collection by the Swedish writer Tomas Tranströmer. It was Tranströmer's debut book: he had previously only been published in journals.[1] The book was well received in the Swedish press and praised for its formal confidence and imagination in metaphors.[2]


Several of the poems in 17 poems have been set to music.[3][4]

***The Sorrow Gondola*** (Template:Lang-sv) is a 1996 poetry collection by the Swedish writer Tomas Tranströmer. The title refers to the composition *La lugubre gondola* by Franz Liszt. It was the first collection by Tranströmer published after his 1990 stroke. It received the August Prize.[1]



## Reception

[edit]

The book was reviewed in *Publishers Weekly*, where the critic wrote that while the author's stroke is never mentioned explicitly, the collection "centers unmistakably on the controlled anguish that the 66-year-old poet's physical condition--and encroaching mortality--imposes." The review continued: "What saves the collection from morbidness is the formal beauty and remorselessly compressed clarity of the writing. Indeed, the almost telegraphic brevity of the poems is the volume's only concession to Transtromer's handicap. With the exception of the four-page title poem, a meditation on Wagner's final months, most of the pieces are only a few stanzas long, yet they retain all the force of the poet's earlier work."[2]

<title>The Great Enigma</title>
<fragment>
*Svenska Dagbladet'*s critic wrote: "When reading [the first five poems] you are delighted by the natural easiness which always has characterised Tranströmer's poetry, in the following haikus by the formal restraint and discipline which makes up the other side of his authorship - not a word too much!" The critic continued: "Tranströmer's new poems are permeated by a completely natural piety. No high tones, no preachment! Only a calm confidence before mortality and a through and through unsentimentally formulated gratitude for being able to exist, to participate."[1]


The book was nominated for the August Prize.[6] In 2007, Frie, whose painting is on the book's cover, collaborated with Tranströmer and exhibited 13 original landscape paintings inspired by the book.[4]

***The Great Enigma*** (Template:Lang-sv) is a 2004 collection of poetry by the Swedish writer Tomas Tranströmer. It consists of five poems in free format, followed by 45 haiku in eleven suites. It is one of the two collections Tranströmer wrote after his 1990 stroke, and it was therefore written at a slow pace with the left hand. It was published in English in 2006.

***17 Poems*** (Template:Lang-sv) is a 1954 poetry collection by the Swedish writer Tomas Tranströmer. It was Tranströmer's debut book: he had previously only been published in journals.[1] The book was well received in the Swedish press and praised for its formal confidence and imagination in metaphors.[2]


Several of the poems in 17 poems have been set to music.[3][4]

<title>Swedish Modernist poetry</title>
<fragment>

The arguably most famous Swedish poet of the 20th century is otherwise Tomas Tranströmer (1931–2015). His poetry is distinguished by a Christian mysticism, moving on the verge between dream and reality, the physical and the metaphysical.[6]



## Notes and references

[edit]

1. **^** \* Lönnroth, L., Delblanc S., Göransson, S. *Den svenska litteraturen* (ed.), 3 volumes (1999)
2. ^ ***a*** ***b*** ***c*** ***d*** *Lundkvist, Martinsson, Ekelöf*, by Espmark & Olsson, in Delblanc, Lönnroth, Göransson, vol 3
3. **^** Algulin, p.230-231
4. **^** Lars Lönnroth, 
Sven Delblanc *Den svenska litteraturen V*, 1989 p.35-40
5. **^** Lars Lönnroth,

</fragment>
<fragment>

Artur Lundkvist played a vital role in promoting modernist poetry in Sweden. His poetry was influenced by surrealism, Walt Whitman and spanish language poets like Lorca and Pablo Neruda.[2]


Karin Boye was one of the most important modernist poets in the 1920s and 1930s with collections like *Moln* (1922), *Gömda land* (1925), *Härdarna* (1927) and *För trädets skull* (1935).[4]


Hjalmar Gullberg (1898–1961) wrote many mystical and Christianity influenced collections, such as *Andliga övningar* (Spiritual Exercises, 1932), but continued to develop and published his greatest work, *Ögon, läppar* (Eyes, Lips), in 1959. 


In the 1940s Erik Lindegren become one of the leading modernist poets with the surreal "blown-up sonnets" of *mannen utan väg* (The man without a way, 1942) and the more romantic *Sviter* (Suites, 1947), a collection that is considered to be the highpoint of 1940s Swedish poetry.[5]


</fragment>

Tomas Tranströmer has this ability to draw out the great and wonderful from the mundane. Since his writing debut in the 1950s with *17 dikter* ("17 Poems", 1954) and *Hemligheter på vägen* ("Secrets on the Way", 1958), Tranströmer's poetry has been characterized by its "everyday roots", and a striving after simplicity that allows room for its reader to marvel and to concentrate.[2] His poems are marked by rich, keen and original imagery. Two of Tranströmer's greatest interests, nature and music, have also left deep impressions on his writing. His famous literary collections include *Östersjöar* ("Baltics", 1974), *För levande och döda* ("For the Living and the Dead", 1989), *Sorgegondolen* ("The Sorrow Gondola", 1996), and *Den stora gåtan* ("The Great Enigma", 2004).[4][3]

He's writing about death, he's writing about history and memory, and nature."[8][11] Prime Minister of Sweden Fredrik Reinfeldt said he was "happy and proud" at the news of Tranströmer's achievement.[12] Meanwhile, international response to the award has been mixed.[13] The prize announcement led to the immediate reissuing of at least two volumes of Tranströmer's poetry.[14][15]

## History

[edit]

Albert Bonnier (1820–1900) established the company in 1837 in Stockholm. Under his son and successor Karl Otto Bonnier (1856–1941), the company grew to be one of the largest publishers in Sweden. Many well-known Swedish authors have been published by Albert Bonniers Förlag. Notable authors have included August Strindberg, Verner von Heidenstam, Gustaf Fröding, Selma Lagerlöf and Hjalmar Söderberg.[3][4][5]


Albert Bonniers Förlag publishes around 100 books per year.[1] Its publications have been characterized by versatility, including novels, poetry, memoirs, biographies, essays and travelogues as well as a variety of non-fiction books.
Contemporary writers include Tomas Tranströmer, Carlos Ruiz Zafón, Dan Brown and Åsa Larsson.[1][6]

<title>Swedish Modernist poetry</title>
<fragment>

The arguably most famous Swedish poet of the 20th century is otherwise Tomas Tranströmer (1931–2015). His poetry is distinguished by a Christian mysticism, moving on the verge between dream and reality, the physical and the metaphysical.[6]



## Notes and references

[edit]

1. **^** \* Lönnroth, L., Delblanc S., Göransson, S. *Den svenska litteraturen* (ed.), 3 volumes (1999)
2. ^ ***a*** ***b*** ***c*** ***d*** *Lundkvist, Martinsson, Ekelöf*, by Espmark & Olsson, in Delblanc, Lönnroth, Göransson, vol 3
3. **^** Algulin, p.230-231

6. **^** *Poeten dold i Bilden*, Lilja & Schiöler, in Lönnroth, Delblanc & Göransson (ed.), vol 3, pp.342-370


</fragment>
<fragment>
* Algulin, Ingemar, *A History of Swedish Literature*, published by the Swedish Institute, 1989. ISBN 91-520-0239-X
* Gustafson, Alrik, *A History of Swedish Literature* (2 volumes), 1961.
* Lönnroth, L., Delblanc S., Göransson, S. *Den svenska litteraturen* (ed.), 3 volumes (1999)
* Swedish Institute, *Modern Literature*, accessed October 17, 2006
* Tigerstedt, E.N., *Svensk litteraturhistoria* (Tryckindustri AB, Solna, 1971)


</fragment>
<fragment>

Artur Lundkvist played a vital role in promoting modernist poetry in Sweden. His poetry was influenced by surrealism, Walt Whitman and spanish language poets like Lorca and Pablo Neruda.[2]


Karin Boye was one of the most important modernist poets in the 1920s and 1930s with collections like *Moln* (1922), *Gömda land* (1925), *Härdarna* (1927) and *För trädets skull* (1935).[4]


Hjalmar Gullberg (1898–1961) wrote many mystical and Christianity influenced collections, such as *Andliga övningar* (Spiritual Exercises, 1932), but continued to develop and published his greatest work, *Ögon, läppar* (Eyes, Lips), in 1959. 


In the 1940s Erik Lindegren become one of the leading modernist poets with the surreal "blown-up sonnets" of *mannen utan väg* (The man without a way, 1942) and the more romantic *Sviter* (Suites, 1947), a collection that is considered to be the highpoint of 1940s Swedish poetry.[5]


</fragment>
<fragment>
**Swedish modernist poetry** developed in the 1910s with authors such as Pär Lagerkvist and was established the 1930s and 1940s. Distinguishing features where experimentation within a variety of styles, usually free prose without rhymes or metric syllables. 


Leading modernistic poets were Artur Lundkvist (1906–1991), Gunnar Ekelöf (1907–1968), Edith Södergran (1892–1923), Karin Boye (1900–1941), Harry Martinson (1904–1978) and Erik Lindegren (1910–1968).[1]


Gunnar Ekelöf has become described as Sweden's first surrealistic poet, after he debuted with the poetry collection *sent på jorden* in 1932, a work was too unconventional to become appreciated.[2] But Ekelöf moved towards romanticism and got betters reviews for his second poetry collection *Dedikation* in 1934. A work that became influential for later Swedish poets was his *Färjesång* in 1941, a finely expressed blend of romanticism, surrealism and the dark clouds of the ongoing World War II.[2]


</fragment>
</document>

*Färjesång* (1941), showed influence from T.S. Eliot, whose poem *East Coker* Ekelöf had translated to Swedish. It took influence from oriental poetry and the darkness of the ongoing Second World War.[4] This was followed by the acclaimed works,[5] the prose book *Promenader* (1941, "Walks"), the disillusioned[4] *Non Serviam* (1945) (its Latin title meaning "I will not serve") and *Om hösten* (1951, "In autumn"). This last included the well-known[4] poem "Röster under jorden" ("Underground voices").[4] In *Strountes* (1955), from Swedish "strunt" ("nonsense"), Ekelöf returned to his attacks on literary conventions, exploring meaninglessness. With his continual wordplay, he demonstrated that meaning can emerge from apparent nonsense.[4]


</fragment>

## History

[edit]

Albert Bonnier (1820–1900) established the company in 1837 in Stockholm. Under his son and successor Karl Otto Bonnier (1856–1941), the company grew to be one of the largest publishers in Sweden. Many well-known Swedish authors have been published by Albert Bonniers Förlag. Notable authors have included August Strindberg, Verner von Heidenstam, Gustaf Fröding, Selma Lagerlöf and Hjalmar Söderberg.[3][4][5]


Albert Bonniers Förlag publishes around 100 books per year.[1] Its publications have been characterized by versatility, including novels, poetry, memoirs, biographies, essays and travelogues as well as a variety of non-fiction books.
Contemporary writers include Tomas Tranströmer, Carlos Ruiz Zafón, Dan Brown and Åsa Larsson.[1][6]

<title>Swedish literature</title>
<fragment>
Arguably the most famous Swedish poet of the 20th century is Tomas Tranströmer (1931–2015). His poetry is distinguished by a Christian mysticism, moving on the verge between dream and reality, the physical and the metaphysical.[54] At the same time there in the Sixties developed a strong tradition influenced by the historical avant-garde, and the Swedish movement of concrete poetry became one of the three global representants for experimental poetry at this time, with representatives like Öyvind Fahlström (who seemingly published the first manifesto for concrete poetry in the world 1954: "Hätila ragulpr på fåtskliaben"),[55] Åke Hodell, Bengt Emil Johnson, and Leif Nylén. In a reaction against the experimental Sixties one in the Seventies took up the beat-tradition from the US, in a continued avant-garde effort which resulted in little magazines publishing poetry, a stencil movement out of which one of Swedish main poets of today – Bruno K. 
</fragment>
<fragment>

Klas Östergren had a major breakthrough with the novel *Gentlemen* in 1980. A prolific author of epic novels as well as short stories Östergren became regarded as one of the leading writers.[48] Majgull Axelsson was noted for the novel *Aprilhäxan* (*April Witch*, 1997) that mixed social realism with magic realism. Autobiographical and confessional writing had an upswing with writers such as Agneta Pleijel, Ernst Brunner and Carina Rydberg. Peter Kihlgård, Sigrid Combüchen and Inger Edelfeldt appeared as other prolific prose writers.[45]



#### Poetry

[edit]

Main article: Swedish Modernist poetry

![](image)Tomas Tranströmer, 2014.
In the 1930s and 1940s, poetry was influenced by the ideals of modernism. Distinguishing features included the desire to experiment, and to try a variety of styles, usually free verse without rhyme or metre.


</fragment>
<fragment>

In the late 19th and early 20th century, Scandinavian literature made its first impression on world literature. From Sweden, the main name was August Strindberg, but Ola Hansson, Selma Lagerlöf and Victoria Benedictsson also attained wider recognition.[28]


The breakthrough of realism in Sweden occurred in 1879. That year, August Strindberg (1845–1912) published *The Red Room* (*Röda Rummet*), a satirical novel that relentlessly attacked the political, the academic, the philosophical and the religious worlds.[29][30]


August Strindberg was a writer world-famous for his dramas and prose, noted for his exceptional talent and complex intellect. He would continue to write several books and dramas until his death in Stockholm.[29][30] He also was an accomplished painter and photographer.[31]

This last included the well-known[4] poem "Röster under jorden" ("Underground voices").[4] In *Strountes* (1955), from Swedish "strunt" ("nonsense"), Ekelöf returned to his attacks on literary conventions, exploring meaninglessness. ## 瑞典文学中保守与进步元素之间的相互作用

瑞典文学界确实存在既保守又重视立传统的力量，这些力量有时会与更具创新性和实验性的文学趋势之间产生张力。这种动态在瑞典的现代文学史中起着重要作用：

**文学出版中的传统力量：**
- 以Albert Bonniers Förlag为代表的主要出版机构成立于1837年，已成为瑞典文学界的重要力量
- 该出版社出版了许多经典瑞典作家，包括August Strindberg、Verner von Heidenstam、Gustaf Fröding、Selma Lagerlöf和Hjalmar Söderberg
- 尽管也出版现代作家如Tomas Tranströmer，但这类著名机构往往在维持文学延续性方面发挥作用

**瑞典文学史上保守与进步之间的张力：**
1. **现代主义时期（1930年代-1940年代）**：维基百科指出这一时期诗歌出现了显著转变，特点是进行实验和尝试多种风格，通常是自由诗，不重韵律和格律。这种实验性可能会与更传统的文学期望产生冲突。

2. **1960年代先锋派：** 一个受历史先锋派影响的强大传统得到发展，瑞典的具体诗歌运动成为当时全球实验诗歌的三大代表之一。这种激进的实验与更保守的文学形式对立。

3. **1970年代的反動回应：** 作为对1960年代实验性的反对，一些作家的发展表现为延续美国的垮掉的一代传统，体现了文学趋向上的典型摆动反應。

**瑞典诗学思想中的二元对立：**
- 2011年诺贝尔奖得主Tomas Tranströmer的作品被描述为“基督教神秘主义，在梦与现实、物质与形而上之间游移”，展现了一种超越简单进步/保守二元对立的精神和务实的路径。

- 那些承继更传统方式的作家，比如Erik Axel Karlfeldt（1931年诺贝尔奖得主），其“高度象征主义的诗歌以地域主义呈现”，表明传统形式如何包含创新的底层内容。

**文学机构的影响：**
瑞典文學院和诺贝尔奖委员会等機構一直是這種緊張關係的重要中介，既獎勵創新（如Tranströmer），也肯定扎根於傳統的作家（如Karlfeldt）。

瑞典文学界从来没有极端的分裂；更可能的是，传统与实验之间的对话持续丰富着文化的文学图景。所谓“保守派”的存在不仅仅是抵制变革的堡垒，而是一个关于什么样的文学表达才构成真正强大和有意义瑞典文学的持续对话的重要参与方。

Based on my searches, I can provide you with information about Tomas Tranströmer (1931-2015) and his place in Swedish literary tradition:

## Tomas Tranströmer's Literary Context

**Major Works and Publishing:**
- First debuted with *17 dikter* ("17 Poems") in 1954
- His collected poetry spans collections like *Östersjöar* ("Baltics", 1974), *För levande och döda* ("For the Living and the Dead", 1989), *Sorgegondolen* ("The Sorrow Gondola", 1996), and *Den stora gåtan* ("The Great Enigma", 2004)
- Published by Albert Bonniers Förlag, a major Swedish publishing house founded in 1837 that has historically published both traditional and modern Swedish authors

## Swedish Literary Tradition: Conservation vs. Innovation

The Swedish literary field has historically featured tension between conservative, tradition-based forces and more experimental approaches:

**Traditional/Conservative Elements:**
- Publishing institutions like Albert Bonniers Förlag have historically played roles in maintaining literary continuity
- The Swedish Academy and Nobel Committee often mediate between tradition and innovation
- Earlier Nobel laureates like Erik Axel Karlfeldt (1931) represented highly symbolic, regional-based poetry

**Modernist/Experimental Forces:**
- Swedish modernist poetry developed in the 1910s with experimental, free verse styles without traditional rhyme or meter
- Leading modernist poets included Gunnar Ekelöf (1907-1968), Artur Lundkvist (1906-1991), Karin Boye (1900-1941), and Erik Lindegren (1910-1968)
- The 1960s saw specific poetry movements that became one of three global representatives of experimental poetry

## Tranströmer's Position

Tranströmer occupies a distinctive middle ground in this tradition. His poetry is characterized as "Christian mysticism, moving on the verge between dream and reality, the physical and the metaphysical." The Nobel Committee specifically noted that he gives "fresh access to reality" through "condensed, translucent images."

Rather than being purely experimental or traditional, Tranströmer's work represents what the Swedish Academy's Peter Englund described as "quite a small production, really" that addresses "big questions" about "death, history and memory, and nature" through everyday experience.

## Critical Perspectives

While I couldn't locate specific references to "Harriet Hues" or detailed New Yorker critiques about Swedish literary rigidity, the historical pattern shows Swedish literature continuously negotiating between:

1. Strong regional/linguistic traditions
2. International modernist influences  
3. Institutional authority (academy, Nobel Committee)
4. Underground/experimental movements

The Swedish literary establishment has proven capable of recognizing both traditional excellence (Karlfeldt) and innovative voices like Tranströmer, suggesting more flexibility than pure rigidity. Tranströmer's Nobel Prize in 2011 demonstrates how institutions can reward work that bridges traditional concerns with accessible, image-based poetry that speaks to contemporary readers.

<title>2011 Nobel Prize in Literature</title>
<fragment>
Tomas Tranströmer has this ability to draw out the great and wonderful from the mundane. Since his writing debut in the 1950s with *17 dikter* ("17 Poems", 1954) and *Hemligheter på vägen* ("Secrets on the Way", 1958), Tranströmer's poetry has been characterized by its "everyday roots", and a striving after simplicity that allows room for its reader to marvel and to concentrate.[2] His poems are marked by rich, keen and original imagery. Two of Tranströmer's greatest interests, nature and music, have also left deep impressions on his writing. His famous literary collections include *Östersjöar* ("Baltics", 1974), *För levande och döda* ("For the Living and the Dead", 1989), *Sorgegondolen* ("The Sorrow Gondola", 1996), and *Den stora gåtan* ("The Great Enigma", 2004).[4][3]

Tranströmer was born in Stockholm in 1931 and raised by his mother Helmy, a schoolteacher, following her divorce from his father, Gösta Tranströmer, an editor.[5][6] He received his secondary education at the Södra Latin Gymnasium in Stockholm, where he began writing poetry. In addition to selected journal publications, his first collection of poems, *17 Poems*, was published in 1954. He continued his education at Stockholm University, graduating as a psychologist in 1956 with additional studies in history, religion and literature.[7] Between 1960 and 1966, Tranströmer split his time between working as a psychologist at the Roxtuna center for juvenile delinquents (sv) and writing poetry.[5] He also worked as a psychologist at the Labor Market Institute in Västerås from 1965 to 1990.[8]

<document>
<title>Swedish literature</title>
<fragment>
Arguably the most famous Swedish poet of the 20th century is Tomas Tranströmer (1931–2015). His poetry is distinguished by a Christian mysticism, moving on the verge between dream and reality, the physical and the metaphysical.[54] At the same time there in the Sixties developed a strong tradition influenced by the historical avant-garde, and the Swedish movement of concrete poetry became one of the three global representants for experimental poetry at this time, with representatives like Öyvind Fahlström (who seemingly published the first manifesto for concrete poetry in the world 1954: "Hätila ragulpr på fåtskliaben"),[55] Åke Hodell, Bengt Emil Johnson, and Leif Nylén. In a reaction against the experimental Sixties one in the Seventies took up the beat-tradition from the US, in a continued avant-garde effort which resulted in little magazines publishing poetry, a stencil movement out of which one of Swedish main poets of today – Bruno K. 
</fragment>
<fragment>

Klas Östergren had a major breakthrough with the novel *Gentlemen* in 1980. A prolific author of epic novels as well as short stories Östergren became regarded as one of the leading writers.[48] Majgull Axelsson was noted for the novel *Aprilhäxan* (*April Witch*, 1997) that mixed social realism with magic realism. Autobiographical and confessional writing had an upswing with writers such as Agneta Pleijel, Ernst Brunner and Carina Rydberg. Peter Kihlgård, Sigrid Combüchen and Inger Edelfeldt appeared as other prolific prose writers.[45]



#### Poetry

[edit]

Main article: Swedish Modernist poetry

![](image)Tomas Tranströmer, 2014.
In the 1930s and 1940s, poetry was influenced by the ideals of modernism. Distinguishing features included the desire to experiment, and to try a variety of styles, usually free verse without rhyme or metre.


</fragment>
<fragment>

The literature of the 1950s continued some of the themes of the 1940s but became more ironic and playful with writers such as Lars Gyllensten, Willy Kyrklund and Lars Forssell. Birgitta Trotzig, a major modernist writer whose work focus on existential questions of a religions nature made her breakthrough with *De utsatta* (*The Exposed*) in 1957. Poets associated with the 1950s are Werner Aspenström who became one of the most widely read poets in Sweden and the highly influential Tomas Tranströmer who made his debut in 1954 with *17 dikter* (*17 Poems*).[45]



#### The 1960s and 1970s

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

In the late 19th and early 20th century, Scandinavian literature made its first impression on world literature. From Sweden, the main name was August Strindberg, but Ola Hansson, Selma Lagerlöf and Victoria Benedictsson also attained wider recognition.[28]


The breakthrough of realism in Sweden occurred in 1879. That year, August Strindberg (1845–1912) published *The Red Room* (*Röda Rummet*), a satirical novel that relentlessly attacked the political, the academic, the philosophical and the religious worlds.[29][30]


August Strindberg was a writer world-famous for his dramas and prose, noted for his exceptional talent and complex intellect. He would continue to write several books and dramas until his death in Stockholm.[29][30] He also was an accomplished painter and photographer.[31]

<fragment>
Tomas Tranströmer has this ability to draw out the great and wonderful from the mundane. Since his writing debut in the 1950s with *17 dikter* ("17 Poems", 1954) and *Hemligheter på vägen* ("Secrets on the Way", 1958), Tranströmer's poetry has been characterized by its "everyday roots", and a striving after simplicity that allows room for its reader to marvel and to concentrate.[2] His poems are marked by rich, keen and original imagery. Two of Tranströmer's greatest interests, nature and music, have also left deep impressions on his writing. His famous literary collections include *Östersjöar* ("Baltics", 1974), *För levande och döda* ("For the Living and the Dead", 1989), *Sorgegondolen* ("The Sorrow Gondola", 1996), and *Den stora gåtan* ("The Great Enigma", 2004).[4][3]

<document>
<title>Swedish Modernist poetry</title>
<fragment>

The arguably most famous Swedish poet of the 20th century is otherwise Tomas Tranströmer (1931–2015). His poetry is distinguished by a Christian mysticism, moving on the verge between dream and reality, the physical and the metaphysical.[6]



## Notes and references

[edit]

1. **^** \* Lönnroth, L., Delblanc S., Göransson, S. *Den svenska litteraturen* (ed.), 3 volumes (1999)
2. ^ ***a*** ***b*** ***c*** ***d*** *Lundkvist, Martinsson, Ekelöf*, by Espmark & Olsson, in Delblanc, Lönnroth, Göransson, vol 3
3. **^** Algulin, p.230-231
4. **^** Lars Lönnroth, 
Sven Delblanc *Den svenska litteraturen V*, 1989 p.35-40
5. **^** Lars Lönnroth, 
Sven Delblanc *Den svenska litteraturen V*, 1989 p.226-228
6. **^** *Poeten dold i Bilden*, Lilja & Schiöler, in Lönnroth, Delblanc & Göransson (ed.), vol 3, pp.342-370


</fragment>
<fragment>

Artur Lundkvist played a vital role in promoting modernist poetry in Sweden. His poetry was influenced by surrealism, Walt Whitman and spanish language poets like Lorca and Pablo Neruda.[2]


Karin Boye was one of the most important modernist poets in the 1920s and 1930s with collections like *Moln* (1922), *Gömda land* (1925), *Härdarna* (1927) and *För trädets skull* (1935).[4]


Hjalmar Gullberg (1898–1961) wrote many mystical and Christianity influenced collections, such as *Andliga övningar* (Spiritual Exercises, 1932), but continued to develop and published his greatest work, *Ögon, läppar* (Eyes, Lips), in 1959. 


In the 1940s Erik Lindegren become one of the leading modernist poets with the surreal "blown-up sonnets" of *mannen utan väg* (The man without a way, 1942) and the more romantic *Sviter* (Suites, 1947), a collection that is considered to be the highpoint of 1940s Swedish poetry.[5]


</fragment>
<fragment>
**Swedish modernist poetry** developed in the 1910s with authors such as Pär Lagerkvist and was established the 1930s and 1940s. Distinguishing features where experimentation within a variety of styles, usually free prose without rhymes or metric syllables. 


Leading modernistic poets were Artur Lundkvist (1906–1991), Gunnar Ekelöf (1907–1968), Edith Södergran (1892–1923), Karin Boye (1900–1941), Harry Martinson (1904–1978) and Erik Lindegren (1910–1968).[1]


Gunnar Ekelöf has become described as Sweden's first surrealistic poet, after he debuted with the poetry collection *sent på jorden* in 1932, a work was too unconventional to become appreciated.[2] But Ekelöf moved towards romanticism and got betters reviews for his second poetry collection *Dedikation* in 1934. A work that became influential for later Swedish poets was his *Färjesång* in 1941, a finely expressed blend of romanticism, surrealism and the dark clouds of the ongoing World War II.[2]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Edith Södergran did not achieve fame during her lifetime, but is today regarded as one of the foremost modernistic poets from the Nordic countries, and she has been translated into all major languages. Her first poetry collection was *Dikter* in 1916, but it was her second collection, *Septemberlyran* (1918) that caught the attention of a larger audience. It is distinguished by a kind of beauty that had not been seen for a long time. Södergran suffered from tuberculosis, which took her life as early as 1923.[2]


Harry Martinson had an unparalleled feeling of nature, in the spirit of Linnaeus. As typical for his generation, he wrote with a free prosody, not bound by rhymes and syllables. A classic work was the autobiographical *Flowering Nettles*, in 1935. His most remarkable work was however *Aniara*, 1956, a story of a spaceship drifting through space.[3]
